title: How he got into the WPA band through his brother-in-law and Mr. Martinez
summary: Brother-in-law Eddie Johnson brought him to sit in; bandleader Joe Martinez, a classical pianist, helped him get hired.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: The Depression years and the WPA band

blocks.x: All right. Well, I'm going to tell you how to come to get in the band, you know? Yeah, go ahead. Well, at that time, they wasn't hiring anybody more in the WPA band because the WPA band was on their way, that is the whole WPA was on their way out because of what was it? Yeah. See? Okay. Because I'll never forget, in 1941, December 7, 1941, my wife and I were sitting on the end of the bed when they declared war. It was on a Sunday. Yeah, I remember that. It was straight. Well, I was still on a boat with Pichon. Okay. Well, they weren't hiring anybody in the WPA band. Well, after I left the boat, my brother-in-law was in there, Eddie Johnson. We call him Eddie Johnson, but his name is Edward Johnson. He played saxophone in the WPA band. And he was a guy, you could give him a flute part, piccolo, oboe, any part, and he transported it to the only saxophone like that, on sight reading. See? Well, we married two sisters. Well, that is, matter of fact, that's my wife's brother-in-law, you know, instead of mine. But, you know, we call it down in New Orleans, you understand? Yeah. I said, well, we're a brother-in-law, see? So, well, matter of fact, he's the one that enticed me to come. He said, well, you ain't doing nothing nice. I said, why don't you come and play with the band? You know? I said, well, all right. That's how, when I got in the band, I said, I come and meet Luis Dumaine, Joe Howard. Oh, man, I knew all them guys. Manuel Paul. Yeah. Manuel Paul. I learned a lot of them. Yeah.
Well, I just can't think about all those guys right now, but I mean, I'll call some- I'll call some-
Harrison Barnes in at them when you were trombone-
No, no, no, no, no, I know.
Eddie Morris, he was in at Bunnheim too.

Well, Eddie Morris, I didn't know him. I didn't know him. Matter of fact, when I joined a band, they had two bands, two dance bands, which consist of about seven men in each band. And that was all the music they had as far as the WPA band was concerned. And they kept that special to play for the soldiers and the sailors at these USO things. See? Well, when I got in the band, well, I used to play at 1420 Canal Street. Matter of fact, I mean, before I got in the band, well, my brother-in-law used to tell me, he said, you ain't doing nothing tonight, why don't you come and sit in with the band? I said, well, you say, you keep your lip up? I said, well, yeah, well, all right. So I used to keep my lip up. I used to go and sit in there. So, who had the bands in charge was Mr. Martinez. He was called Martinez. See? Well, you remember him?
I know of him, Joe Martinez.

Joe, yeah, yeah, yeah. He was living out in Metry. And he was an old classical piano player. And that man, as long as I've been in that band, I think he touched the piano one time, and that was the show off. He called himself showing off. You understand? And with that band, played some kind of classical stuff. It was remarkable. And he said he never touched the piano. He said he might play the piano about once a year. And he was an old fellow at that time. But boy, I mean, the technique he used and everything was wonderful, you know? Well, he used to come in there and he used to ask, say, well, who's that, you know? So my brother-in-law, him and my brother-in-law was kind of good friends, you know? So he'd say, that's my brother-in-law. He'd say, just come and sit up. He'd say, sit in. He'd say to keep his lip up. He'd say, I guess it's all right. He'd say he's a good musician and everything. So Mr. Martinez would say, well, he ain't messing up. He'd say, no, he ain't messing up. He'd say, he's a good musician. He'd just come off the steamer capital. Well, the steamer capital, when you work on the steamer capital, that was a big job. Everybody used to look up at you, you know, when you were working on steamer capital. So I work in the WPA band. That is, I mean, I used to, everywhere they used to play, you know? I used to go and play and play and tell Mr. Martinez got to know me real well. See? Then he used to send, sometimes the other high officials would come on the job and look at him, you know, and then they'd inquire like that, you know? So then jobs was kind of rough to get there at that time, too. See? So I told Mr. Martinez, I said, Mr. Martinez, I said, well, the first break you ever. I said, I'd like to get in the WPA band. He said, you really would like that? I said, sure, I'd like that. So I don't know if he'd seek to get me in there. Well, then I got in the band. As soon as I got in the band, Louis Dumaine, the trumpet player across the river, he was in the band because he was in my band. Louis Dumaine had charge of one band and somebody else had charge of the other band. Well, when I got into the WPA, they put me in charge of the other band and left Louis Dumaine with one band. So Louis Dumaine was the leader of one band and I was the leader of the other band. Charlie Love.
